headline_marked: [[Vinton Cerf, 'Father of the Internet', retires]] from Google after 20 years
headline: Vinton Cerf, 'Father of the Internet', retires from Google after 20 years
summary: Vinton Cerf, co-creator of TCP/IP, is stepping down as Google's chief internet evangelist next week, concluding over two decades with the company and a career that shaped the modern internet.
details: Vinton Cerf, 83, is officially retiring from his role as Google's chief internet evangelist next week, marking the end of a 20-year tenure with the tech giant. He is widely recognized as a co-architect of the internet's foundational TCP/IP protocols.

Cerf's groundbreaking work, alongside Robert Kahn, began in the 1970s and led to the development of the basic rules that allow different computer networks to communicate. This fundamental contribution has earned him numerous accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom and a Turing Award.

During a recent conference, Cerf shared his predictions for the future of AI, anticipating that autonomous AI agents will necessitate new interoperability standards. He emphasized the critical need for precision beyond natural language for effective inter-agent communication.

This push for standardization could lead to certain companies defining early protocols gaining significant influence, a dynamic reminiscent of the early internet's protocol wars. Cerf's insights highlight the ongoing evolution of digital infrastructure, even as he steps back from his official role.
caption:
After two decades at Google and a lifetime shaping the digital world, Vinton Cerf, co-creator of the internet's TCP/IP protocols, is retiring.

Vinton Cerf, 83, is officially retiring from his role as Google's chief internet evangelist next week, marking the end of a 20-year tenure with the tech giant. He is widely recognized as a co-architect of the internet's foundational TCP/IP protocols.

Cerf's groundbreaking work, alongside Robert Kahn, began in the 1970s and led to the development of the basic rules that allow different computer networks to communicate. This fundamental contribution has earned him numerous accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom and a Turing Award.

During a recent conference, Cerf shared his predictions for the future of AI, anticipating that autonomous AI agents will necessitate new interoperability standards. He emphasized the critical need for precision beyond natural language for effective inter-agent communication.

This push for standardization could lead to certain companies defining early protocols gaining significant influence, a dynamic reminiscent of the early internet's protocol wars. Cerf's insights highlight the ongoing evolution of digital infrastructure, even as he steps back from his official role.

headline_marked: US [[ends 50-year ban]] on supersonic flight over land
headline: US ends 50-year ban on supersonic flight over land
summary: New noise limits replace the prohibition on overland supersonic flight, allowing faster-than-sound travel as long as the boom is below a set level.
details: The U.S. Department of Transportation has taken a significant step to repeal a 50-year ban on supersonic flight over land, a move driven by advancements in aviation technology that promise to mitigate the disruptive sonic booms.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) published a notice to replace the ban with a noise-based standard. This means aircraft can fly faster than Mach 1 over U.S. territory, provided the resulting noise remains within a specified limit.
This action follows an executive order from President Trump in June 2025, directing the FAA to remove regulatory barriers hindering supersonic aviation and establish new noise standards.

Since 1973, civil aircraft have been prohibited from exceeding Mach 1 over U.S. land due to public opposition to the loud sonic booms, which in the past caused property damage and widespread complaints.
The FAA aims to finalize these rules by mid-2027, with Administrator Bryan Bedford stating that technological progress will "eliminate the old sonic boom" and minimize noise impacts on communities.

Companies like Boom Supersonic and Spike Aerospace are developing new generations of supersonic passenger jets, with Boom's Overture jets already having pre-orders from major airlines like United, American, and Japan Airlines.
